adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Audio guide, stop seven: the story of the thermometer.

For most of human history, people judged heat by touch. A baker knew his oven was ready when a handful of flour turned brown in a few seconds. A blacksmith judged the temperature of iron by its color, from a dull cherry red to a bright orange white. These methods were practical, but they were personal, and they did not travel well. Two craftsmen in neighboring towns could disagree about whether a fire was hot enough for the same task, and neither could prove the other wrong.

The first serious instruments appeared in the seventeenth century, when glassblowers learned to draw fine tubes and seal them at one end. Early thermometers were filled with water, then with alcohol, and finally with mercury, which expands evenly and stays liquid across a wide range of temperatures. Each maker chose his own scale, so the readings on one instrument meant little on another. A physician in Padua might record a fever as a certain number of degrees, while a colleague in London recorded the same fever differently.

The turning point came when Daniel Fahrenheit and Anders Celsius each proposed fixed points that anyone could reproduce. Fahrenheit used a mixture of ice, water, and salt for his lower mark, and the heat of a healthy body for his upper one. Celsius took a different route: he anchored his scale to the freezing and boiling points of pure water, which were easy to observe almost anywhere in the world. His original scale actually ran the other way, with zero at the boiling point and one hundred at freezing, but later users reversed it, and the familiar version we use today was born.

Visitors often ask why water was chosen as the reference substance. The answer is simple. Water is everywhere, it is cheap, and its changes of state are dramatic and repeatable. Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level, and that single fact gave nineteenth-century scientists a shared landmark for calibrating their instruments. Cooks benefited too. A recipe written in Naples could be followed in Stockholm, at least in principle, because both kitchens could agree on what a hard rolling boil looked like. Even today, a kitchen thermometer is checked against the same fixed points that Celsius described.

Altitude complicates the picture, and every mountain walker learns the lesson sooner or later. As a climber gains height, the column of air above her grows shorter, and the pressure on the surface of a pot falls with it. The boiling point drops as well, so vegetables take longer to soften and tea tastes weaker. On the summit of Mont Blanc, roughly four thousand eight hundred metres above the sea, the effect is easy to notice. Guides sometimes demonstrate it by dipping a thermometer into a steaming pot and passing it around.

Pressure works in the other direction. Inside a sealed cooker, steam cannot escape, and the pressure rises above the ordinary atmospheric value. The water then reaches a higher temperature before it begins to bubble, which is why stews cook faster in a pressure cooker than in an open pan. Industrial chemists exploit the same principle when they heat a reaction under controlled pressure, and engineers who design boilers must keep the relationship between pressure and temperature firmly in mind.

The modern thermometer no longer depends on mercury, and digital sensors have replaced glass tubes in most laboratories. Yet the old fixed points remain useful, because they are reproducible and easy to explain. Every student who calibrates a sensor is repeating an experiment that is three hundred years old, and the lesson has not changed: measure carefully, choose a reference that anyone can check, and record what you did so that others can follow.
